bib.title: From Prompt Injections to Protocol Exploits: Threats in LLM-Powered AI Agents Workflows

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "From Prompt Injections to Protocol Exploits: Threats in LLM-Powered AI Agents Workflows", Ferrag, Tihanyi, Hamouda, Maglaras, Lakas, Debbah. arXiv:2506.23260v2 [cs.CR], 14 Dec 2025 (IEEE-style preprint). The text mentions expert review but names no venue.

COVERAGE: 204,731 of 204,731 chars (all 36 pages) read, including the references. Nothing skipped. No unread page ranges. Extraction was clean text. Equations and tables are slightly mangled but readable.

CLAIMS (ranked for the execution-boundaries note)

- claim: The survey's own threat-feasibility table says input manipulation and protocol attacks need little privilege and are highly feasible. They hit the tool, agent and protocol layers, so the boundary between agent and tool is the main exposure.
  number: Input manipulation needs privilege "None to Low" and feasibility "High". Protocol vulnerabilities need "Low to Medium" privilege and are "High" feasibility.
  setup: A qualitative author judgement. Not measured.
  quote: "Protocol Vulnerabilities (e.g., MCP, ACP, ANP, A2A Exploits) Low to Medium (connector, API, or communication access) High — affects integration boundaries and message exchanges between agents Protocol / Agent"
  where: Table VI, p.27

- claim: Adaptive attacks bypassed all eight tested prompt-injection defences for tool-using agents. This is the strongest evidence in the survey that prompt-level defences alone are not a boundary.
  number: 8 defences, each bypassed, ASR >50% each
  setup: Reported from Zhan et al. 2025 (indirect prompt injection against tool-using LLM agents). The survey says ASR values come from the original papers and "are not directly comparable".
  quote: "The authors evaluate eight existing defense mechanisms and demonstrate that all can be bypassed by adaptive attack strategies, resulting in an attack success rate exceeding 50% in each case."
  where: Sec III-B4, p.10

- claim: The Toxic Agent Flow exploit on GitHub's MCP server is the flagship real incident. A malicious issue in a public repo makes the agent pull private repo data into context and leak it in a public PR. The survey says alignment and prompt-injection defences did not stop it, and the proposed mitigations are granular permission controls plus monitoring.
  number: none
  setup: Invariant Labs, May 2025 blog (ref [51]), described second-hand. Agent holds read/write tools over both public and private repos.
  quote: "This attack demonstrates the limitations of traditional security measures, including model alignment and prompt injection defenses, which fail to prevent such manipulations. The paper also proposes mitigation strategies, including the enforcement of granular permission controls and continuous security monitoring"
  where: Sec III-B5, p.10; Fig. 5, p.12; Table V

- claim: The paper lists 2025 CVEs in agent tooling, including a sandbox escape in OpenAI Codex CLI and OS command execution via untrusted MCP endpoints. It says most exploit insecure interfaces, permissive plugin logic or protocol flaws, often with low privilege.
  number: 11 CVEs in Table VIII, including CVE-2025-59532 (Codex CLI v0.2.0-0.38.0, sandbox escape), CVE-2025-6514 (MCP-Remote v0.0.5-0.1.15, OS command execution via untrusted MCP endpoints) and CVE-2025-49596 (MCP Inspector v0.14.0, CSRF/DNS-rebinding RCE)
  setup: Mapped by the authors to their four categories. The Codex CLI CVE is filed under "Model Compromise", which looks like a stretch (CWE-20). No exploitation rates given.
  quote: "Sandbox escape via directory control flaw allows arbitrary file execution."
  where: Table VIII, p.31; discussion p.30-31

- claim: MCP-layer attack vectors the paper names. Prompt injection leads to unauthorised tool calls. Replay and DoS come through infinite tool-call loops. Credential theft comes through confused-deputy proxy abuse. SQL injection comes through unvalidated tool arguments.
  number: none
  setup: Illustrative TypeScript snippet, not a measured exploit.
  quote: "Fig. 15 highlights a critical vulnerability in the MCP TypeScript SDK where unvalidated user input is passed directly into the 'args.query' field and subsequently executed by the database."
  where: Sec VI-B, p.30; Fig. 15

- claim: A protocol threat matrix pairs each attack with a mitigation, mostly classic security controls. These are useful as a checklist for execution boundaries.
  number: none
  setup: Author-compiled table for MCP, A2A, ANP, ACP. No evaluation.
  quote: "Insecure Configuration Misconfiguration MCP, A2A, ANP, ACP Unauthorized access Secure defaults; regular audits; least-privilege settings" and "Denial-of-Service (DoS) Resource Exhaustion ... Rate limiting; circuit breakers" and "Credential theft Proxy Abuse ... Token audience binding; explicit delegation checks" and "Capability Escalation Authorization Abuse ANP, ACP Privilege escalation Fine-grained ACLs; runtime authorization checks"
  where: Table VII, p.28-29. Other rows: replay (nonce/timestamp, unique message IDs), token theft (short-lived tokens, mTLS), supply chain (code signing, integrity monitoring), cross-agent prompt injection (input isolation, per-agent validation).

- claim: Recursive task spawning is modelled as a resource-exhaustion attack. Corba spreads across multi-agent topologies using benign-looking instructions. The survey states a cap on task trees and a rate threshold.
  number: none (formal: rate threshold τ_rate, resource cap τ_cap)
  setup: Corba (Zhou et al. 2025) tested on AutoGen and Camel. The survey gives no ASR for it.
  quote: "creating unbounded task trees|T| → ∞. If resource consumption exceedsτ cap, the orchestrator halts or crashes, leading to distributed denial of service across the A2A network."
  where: Sec VI-A5, p.29; Sec V-C1, p.25

- claim: The future-work list for MCP SDKs reads as a hardening checklist. It names least privilege, mutual auth and encryption, schema validation, runtime anomaly monitoring, provenance logs, sandboxing plugin execution and auditing dependencies. Mitigations in this part are listed, not tested.
  number: none
  quote: "developers should adopt mitigation-oriented engineering practices such as enforcing least-privilege permissions, using mutual authentication and encrypted communications, validating structured data schemas, monitoring runtime anomalies, and maintaining cryptographically verifiable provenance logs. Furthermore, sandboxing plugin execution and auditing dependencies helps prevent malicious package injection"
  where: Sec VII-I, p.34

- claim: Static access control cannot keep up with agents. The paper proposes runtime-negotiated least-privilege policies and time-boxed per-tool-call permissions, plus attested context provenance and formal verification. These are research directions.
  number: none
  quote: "Traditional static access controls cannot keep pace with the fluid, language-driven workflows that modern agents require. Future research should explore declarative policy languages that allow hosts to negotiate and update least-privilege rules at runtime"
  where: Sec VII-A, p.31

- claim: Attack success numbers in the survey's headline table. Treat them as author-reported and not comparable.
  number: Adaptive IPI >=50%. Compositional Instruction Attack >95% (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama2-70b-chat). GPTFuzz >90%. GAP 92% on GPT-3.5 using 54% of the queries. AEIA 93% on AndroidWorld. Composite Backdoor 100% at 3% poisoning (LLaMA-7B, Emotion dataset). PoisonedRAG 90% with 5 injected texts in a store of millions.
  quote: "At-tack Success Rates (ASR) values are reported as stated in the original publications. These results are not directly comparable due to variations in model architectures, datasets, experimental setups, and defense mechanisms."
  where: Intro, p.2, Table I; Tables III-V

- claim: Fine-tuning-based defences beat prompt-based defences against context manipulation in Web3 agents. The text says prompt defences are ineffective.
  number: CrAIBench has more than 150 tasks and over 500 attack test cases. No ASR figure is given.
  setup: ElizaOS Web3 agents. The gain is said to hold for single-step tasks only.
  quote: "while prompt-based defenses are ineffective against context manipulation, fine-tuning-based defenses provide more robust protection, substantially reducing attack success rates while maintaining utility in single-step tasks."
  where: Sec III-D5, p.15

- claim: Intent-based defence cut compositional-jailbreak ASR. One defensive datapoint.
  number: ">74%" reduction
  quote: "significantly reducing the attack success rate by over 74%"
  where: Sec III-C1, p.11

- claim: Persistent compromise, which sandboxing does not fix. Memory poisoning (MINJA) injects records through queries alone. Backdoored agents stay effective after fine-tuning on clean data. DemonAgent reaches near-100% ASR at 0% detection.
  number: "nearly 100% success while maintaining a 0% detection rate"
  setup: DemonAgent on the AgentBackdoorEval dataset.
  quote: "Experimental results across several datasets show that the attack achieves nearly 100% success while maintaining a 0% detection rate"
  where: Sec IV-B4, p.20; MINJA Sec IV-C4, p.21

LIMITS
- This is a taxonomy survey. It runs no experiments and reports no defence evaluation of its own. Every number is second-hand from the cited papers.
- ASRs mix different models, datasets and defences, and the authors admit they are not comparable. Many cited attacks target chat, text-to-image or training pipelines. They are not tool-execution boundaries.
- The "expert review" and "cross-mapping to incidents" validation is asserted in the abstract and intro with no detail given on reviewers or process.
- Formal "threat models" are generic notation (context C=(h,x,k), safety policy π). They are not used to derive any result.
- Mitigations are listed, not tested. Sandboxing gets one sentence (Sec VII-I) and one table row. There is no comparison of isolation mechanisms such as containers, microVMs or seccomp.
- Table VIII's category labels are debatable. Codex CLI sandbox escape is labelled "Model Compromise".
- The survey misnames MCP in places ("Model-Control-Protocol" in a heading, "Model Control Protocol" in the roadmap). The abstract claims "first" integrated taxonomy.
- MCP and A2A material is current to mid-2025, and CVEs were accessed Oct 2025. The protocol specs have likely changed since.

BUILDS ON
Perez & Ribeiro 2022 (PromptInject); Pedro et al. 2023 (P2SQL in LangChain); Zhan et al. 2025 (adaptive IPI); Invariant Labs, Milanta & Beurer-Kellner 2025 (GitHub MCP); Hou et al. 2025 (MCP landscape and security); Yang et al. 2025 (agent protocol survey); Deng et al. 2025 (AI agents under threat); Anil et al. 2024 (many-shot jailbreaking); Zou et al. 2024 (PoisonedRAG); Yang et al. 2024 (agent backdoor); Dong et al. 2025 (MINJA); Zhou et al. 2025 (Corba); Narajala & Habler 2025 (enterprise MCP security); Habler et al. 2025 (secure A2A). Protocols cited: MCP, A2A (Google), ANP, ACP.

CODE
Fig. 15, p.30. An illustrative injection point. This is an illustrative sketch whose SDK class names (McpClient, StreamableHttpTransport) may not match the real SDK:
```
const response = await client.invoke({
tool: "database_query",
args: {
// <-- Injection point
query: userInput
}
});
...
runQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=123; DROP TABLE users; --");
```

FIGURES
- Fig. 5 (p.12), Toxic Agent Flow. A malicious GitHub issue leads the agent, using get_issues/read_file/write_file, to leak a private repo through a public README or PR. It shows an untrusted-input to privileged-tool to exfiltration chain at a glance.
- Fig. 14 (p.28), a map of attacks onto the MCP and A2A architecture. It shows where each attack sits (host, MCP client/server, A2A server).
- Fig. 15 (p.30), the MCP SQL injection snippet.
- Fig. 7 (p.14), backdoor variants on a shopping agent (query, observation and thought triggers). It shows that internal action changes can hide behind a correct final output.
- Table VII and Table VI (pp.27-29), the mitigation matrix and the privilege/feasibility table. I did not run the figures.py caption script. Descriptions are taken from the extracted caption text.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF text.
- Some sentences in the extraction are garbled, for example the query-free attack paragraph on p.14 and "the number of protests" for demonstrations. Section IV-A repeats the Input Manipulation formal definition (a copy-paste error in the paper). Check any figure that matters against the PDF.
- Page numbers above come from the page counters printed in the extracted text (1-36).
